summary: Concurrency and prioritization primitives used by Fusillade for queueing and serialized work execution.
recommendedPatterns: Use punchclock for bounded, prioritized work queues when concurrency policy matters.
Give queued work meaningful keys and keep tasks idempotent.
avoidPatterns: Do not use punchclock for routine workflows that do not need queueing or prioritization.
Do not hide queue policy in magic numbers.
setupSteps: Add punchclock when advanced queueing is needed.
Define priority and serialization rules explicitly.
commonPitfalls: Using queueing infrastructure where a simpler async flow would do.
Ignoring the need for deterministic keys and cancellation.

packageSelection: Use Punchclock for lean Primitives scheduling and conventional Task APIs.
Use Punchclock.Reactive only for full System.Reactive compatibility.
Prefer Task operations in ordinary application code and observables when stream composition adds value.
sourceGeneratorGuidance: No queue source generator is required; use ReactiveUI.SourceGenerators for command/state boilerplate that submits work.
Use Splat.DependencyInjection.SourceGenerator to register a shared OperationQueue at the composition root.
compatibilityNotes: Queue lifetime and shared ownership must be explicit.
Cancellation, pause/resume, priority, and shutdown behavior should be tested with deterministic sequencing.
migrationGuidance: Switch System.Reactive queue surfaces to Punchclock plus ISequencer by default.
Retain Punchclock.Reactive only where Rx public contracts must remain, and keep that boundary separate from lean pipelines.
